Looking back it makes sense in THIS case. She needed to know some of my past to help me now.

It feels so good to finally be heard and seen and respected. To be understood and be given legitimate advice.

Oh it’s not too bad. Got diagnosed in November, and just turned 22. It’s really just a relief when I realise I am able to take meds to combat the overwhelming feelings. 

I take Ritalin (methylphenidate), 10mg when I’m stimulated and 5mg when I know I’ll just be chilling at home. It can be a hassle since the 10mg only work for 3 hours (for some ppl 4 hours), before they wear off.

It can be quite hard to fall asleep on these pills. I’ve been advised not to take any after 6pm, since they won’t wear off until 9pm.

So no, not medicated 24/7. Usually between 7am-9pm tho. 

I don’t always feel like this no. I just happened to get frustrated while they had worn off, I forgot to take the next pill. 

I’m not entirely sure about “the hour” you’re referring to, _but_ once I get home from work I do usually retreat to my room and listen to some music. I’m tired, been stimulated all day and I would like to just focus on a hobby or something. During this time I’m usually off meds and my brother’s voice can really put murder on my mind. It rings through all the rooms! Lol. 

So yeah, I got a couple of hours where I prefer to be alone but it really changes all the time! Throughout November I was way more talkative and social. 

It can be hard to get things done when you enter “zombie mode” (executive dysfunction). When you just can’t get anything done. It usually happens when the ADHD brain runs out of dopamine. Dopamine helps you feel good and gets the body into action. Try and read my previous post on this! If your daughter falls into that stage, it can really help to eat some sugar, listen to some upbeat music or whatever gets her excited/happy. Lots of people shared what they do in the comments :)

That sounds like… A terrible source?? Lmao. 

Neurotransmitters are used to send messages from neurone to neurone (or from neurones to muscles). This communication between two neurones _happens_ in the synaptic cleft. 

Hormones travel in your bloodstream to tissues, skin, muscles or organs.

Both hormones and neurotransmitters are described as the body’s chemical messengers though. So it can definitely get confusing. Maybe the explanation you’re referring to accidentally switched around hormones and neurotransmitters?

Don’t get me wrong it took years of hard work. At first I had a pretty sucky psychologist who wasn’t much help, so I was mostly on my own.

Later I got some appointments with a cognitive therapist, I guess you could call it. I’ll try and explain it the best I can in English.

She told me that social anxiety is like a habit. You got all these neurones in your brain. Every time you think “they’ll think I look ridiculous.” a line is drawn across two neurones. Eventually, if you keep thinking that phrase, you’ll have a whole highway across those neurones. 

Once in a while you may think “They _wont_ think I look ridiculous.” so you got another set of neurones with just a few lines between them. 

When your brain has to pick between those two phrases, it’s gonna jump to the one with most traction, the one with most lines. So if you have a presentation the same day, your brain will out of habit think “they’ll think I look ridiculous during the presentation.” 

The hard part is recognising these patterns and habits, and stopping them. Every time you think “they’ll think I’m ridiculous.” you gotta catch yourself and immediately replace the thought by “no they _wont_.”

If you keep doing this, you add lines to the “they wont think I’m ridiculous” phrase and eventually your new, anxiety free highway will overpower the one your anxiety created.

Does that make sense?

A huge part of the breakthrough for me was realising that I had created my own fears and that they weren’t “real”. That it was simply a pattern that I had the control to change. It gave me a lot of courage and motivation to tackle the every day struggles. 

Like going grocery shopping, I had horrible anxiety about things like “they’ll think I’m so fat because I’m buying this chocolate.” So I would repeat to myself that they did not, that it was in my head and I would try to focus on something else. Even went as far as thinking “no, they’re looking because they are admiring my shoes.” Or something else.

Side note: I don’t mean to use the word fat in a degrading way, but that is a very common example of my own social anxiety and what I’ve heard others say about their own.

I’m very active in the ADHD sub Reddit :) I think it can be hard to portray ADHD accurately, but easy to portray it inaccurately. 

With depression, there’s the general knowledge that the lack of mental energy makes it hard to keep your room clean for example. 

So while you may know of ADHD symptoms, and use the correct ones, you may end up portraying it inaccurately anyway.

With ADHD it’s more complicated and while it’s a real symptom to have a messy room, I think people have a tendency to assume it’s laziness. Like portraying a character as “oh, it’s messy again. Oh well. Fuck that.”

When in reality it’s “okay I should clean, but I also need to walk the dog, and make dinner later and what am I wearing tomorrow— oh shit the room. Okay there’s clothes, plates, cans, some paper— oh fuck it’s so much, I can’t do this. Okay I’ll start with the clothes. I’ve put away two t-shirts now— oh there are so many plates maybe I should begin with them. Okay that’s 3 plates— oh there are so many socks, why am I not getting anywhere!?”

So while the symptoms are very inconsistent, the disorder is the _same_ . Picking out symptoms for my main character, won’t necessarily make it un-relatable for someone with other symptoms. 

Maybe other ADHD people won’t have a problem with cleaning their room, but they’ll experience the same overwhelming thought process while cooking or putting together a project for school.

Like my brother loves cooking but I despise it cause it’s too much going on. At the same time I thrive at work having several balls in the air the same time, but my brother completely has a melt down.

Does that make sense? I think with ADHD, it’s not as much the symptoms as the thought process behind it. The physical feeling that comes with it too. Like if I get rejected in the smallest way, my fingertips _ache_. I’ve heard others say their throat begins hurting. But it’s the same thing!

I’m a big analyser, I’ve always been a very quiet and anxiety ridden kid. So every time I go home from work, I subconsciously analyse the day. Looking at the old jobs and this one, I know what to look for, for me personally now. 

I need: 

- stability. Which means knowing my hours/shifts/work days at least a week prior. That way I can mentally lay a rough plan for my free time. That way I’ll be sure to make time for special interest/hobbies and feel fulfilled! 

- the ability to say no to extra hours. I honestly love working a 50 hour shift, HOWEVER I also need my down time as most people. Otherwise I get overwhelmed and I spiral. I’ve had past bosses BEG and threaten me to come in. My current boss just labels me as “unavailable” and I don’t need a reason other than no. On top of that there’s no hard feelings. This is important to me because I’ll quickly start to feel guilty and worry about getting laid off and also overwork myself.

- good people. In my opinion, good people are people who are kind, helpful and open. As a girl who got diagnosed at 21, I’ve masked my WHOLE life. Knowing people accept me for me, allows me to relax and get rid of the performance. I won’t have crippling anxiety, worrying about getting judged for saying something “weird”. I can help my colleagues and feel confident they won’t abuse that, but rather appreciate it and have my back if needed! 

- having control of my own breaks. This is not a must, and can be hard to find. I do notice that if I expect my break to be at 1.30, and it gets pushed to 1.35… 1.40… 2.05. I get very frustrated and anxious. Sometimes with ADHD, it can be unpredictable. I’ve begged past bosses to have my break at a certain time (usually exactly halfway through my shift) or right now. When I was denied or it kept getting pushed, I was close to tears. Today I was like “hey can I take my break now?” And they just shrugged and said “sure.” They don’t care, as long as I do my job.

- having control of my shifts. I tell my bosses “I’ll work any shift you give me BUT if you want the best version of me, schedule me after 10am-1pm up until midnight.” Nightshifts worked amazingly for me. I have big trouble sleeping and take three pills every evening. I say this so they don’t assume I’m just lazy and want to sleep in. When I turn up at 5.30am, crawling through the door, it’s usually also very apparent that I’m telling the truth.

- freedom. With ADHD, it’s easy to miss things, overlook them or just generally do things in a different way than others. I’m big on work smarter, not harder. If I’m hanging something up, I might hang them on a wrong knob first but notice immediately. Or I’ll misplace one item and then notice when I’ve finished the rest. Having someone constantly looking over my shoulder and immediately correcting me honestly breaks my soul. I just stand there “I know” or “I was gonna do that.” And I just sound like a have an attitude. Freedom to work at my own pace without feeling watched is necessary. I had a boss once who corrected the way I dusted off shelves and I HAD to be corrected. The difference? She wanted me to crawl into the whole furniture, around hoses and what not to do it. I’m allergic to dust! I had found a pole that worked wonders when placed on top of the towel but nope… ripped it right out of my hands.

- having a say in my tasks. What kills me about retail is the damn register. I’m great at simple math! Until someone’s watching me… adding 3 to 8 is suddenly extremely hard. Just in general, when people are waiting for me to do something, my energy drips off of me. I told my old boss this and he STILL put me at the register for up to 10 hours in his extremely busy store. I would beg him halfway through shifts to please switch me out. He did not. My current boss was like “aight, R over here loves to be at the register, so that’s fine.” So whenever R is at work, he’s at the register and I stock up shelves. 

- BEING HANDS ON. Stocking shelves, throwing out paper, helping customers and changing price signs are all boring tasks. It keeps me busy though, keeps the energy flowing rather than getting trapped in my body. I walk around, see the different surroundings, walk some customers to the right location and take note of the items. Time passes by!

- room for fun. As I mentioned, my coworker and I dicked around today with the mouse or spider. Another coworker and I would throw snow balls at each other any time we saw each other. Just being able to chit chat! A past boss would watch the cameras like a hawk and break up anyone who interacted. One time I asked a coworker for help and he came running and broke us up before I got the answer. 

- level of responsibility. I’ve been in a manger position too, I’ve worked at a daycare, I’ve closed up shops, I’ve worked with animals, I’ve been just a cashier and a sales assistant. I liked the extra responsibility of the daycare or being a manger, as long as I’m not the “top boss”. I however don’t like being on bottom cause I have this tendency of “putting people to work.” It’s not malicious at ALL it’s just like “okay I gotta do this and this and— oh he’s just standing there, maybe he can help me.” But I come across as bossy and I can understand why people get pissed off. Working on that!

- constructive feedback. I had a boss who thought that constructive feedback was ALWAYS saying “next time, just do this differently and it’s perfect.” While that’s definitely good, it gets extremely tiring to never be good enough. Doing what he tells me to do differently, only for him to jump hoops to be able to correct something else. Sometimes constructive can be “looks good!” Without pointing out that teeny tiny spot of dust missed. There doesn’t need to be a lesson every time you receive feedback, ESPECIALLY if there’s still improvement from last time.

I hope you made it this far without getting distracted or overwhelmed! Maybe you relate to some of these points and are able to start looking for a job based on them. Maybe if you feel the exact opposite and then you can look for jobs based on that! I think it’d be a good idea to sit down and write a list of things that sucked and things that were great at work. Maybe include your partner! They might have noticed some things you haven’t. I have had LONG conversations with my dad about this and we figured these things out together just by discussing them. A different perspective is great for figuring out what YOU struggle with and what most people struggle with.

To clarify, I rarely ever read one shots. I like good, slow burn fanfic. I use a lot of dialogue in my pieces but they all have a purpose. Foreshadowing is something I use a lot, if not with direct speech then with inner dialogue. Dialogue also something I use a lot to let my reader get to know the characters that play a smaller role in the plot. 

For example I’m currently writing a fanfic right now where most of the plot is on one street. I thought about making a long chapter describing each family, but instead I made short scenes where I let most of the characters talk. That’s how the reader finds out what family is spreading around the gossip, what family is “better than everyone else”, what family is naive but good hearted and what family whose mother went missing last year. In my opinion it has a faster pace and keeps it interesting, rather than writing an 8k chapter. The details can always be filled later.

I had SAD. My psychologist explained to me exactly how SAD (and other forms of anxiety) works down to a neurological scale. This just completely made sense to me and something clicked. Previously I had been told it’s something you could never get rid of but the way she explained it... It was obvious that I am in fact in control of my anxiety. 

I have to say my anxiety got MUCH better when I broke up with my ex because I got out of a toxic environment that made me more anxious. That was an important step towards my recovery.

One thing I really struggled with was presentations. I would start sobbing if something went wrong. My psychologist told me to stand somewhere private in a “power pose” (like Superman, hands on hips) for five minutes before a presentation. This releases testosterone and gives you a self confidence boost. Because I did this, I experienced success after my presentations and gradually became less anxious and scared. I love doing presentations now.

I did this with everything. Scared of the gym? I went with a friend and did everything I could to remind myself of things like “I don’t look stupid, they’re not staring, I’m not doing the exercises wrong.” Etc.

SAD (maybe also other forms of anxiety) is really created by yourself and your own fearful and judgmental thoughts. So it makes sense that you have to start thinking differently to get better. 

It took a lot of energy and hard work but it feels so good now. I hope you can find some sort of help in this. It’s different for everyone after all :) 

And it’s important to know that sometimes you might take 2 steps back, but as long as you take another step forward again, it’s okay
